name: Pinkish Cinnamon
lede: Pinkish Cinnamon names a warm, pale orange-tan by plain modifier grammar, built on [[cinnamon]], and Robert Ridgway's 1912 plates are the earliest dated record our sources carry for it.

sections.title: A modifier on an older plate
sections.body:
The name follows the modifier pattern "pinkish" plus the parent hue [[cinnamon]] [1]. Robert Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* lists the swatch on plate XXIX, hue 15′′, tone b [2]. Our library separately notes a near-duplicate, Tan (Crayola), about 1.9 units away by measured color, an unrelated brand name rather than a shared origin [3].

The nearest named colors by measured distance are [[apricot-buff]], more vivid, and [[light-cinnamon]] and [[light-cinnamon]], both almost the same shade [4]. [[tumbleweed]] and [[peachbeige]] sit further out, both duller [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive of 23,781 paintings finds a match for this tan in 509 of them, about 2.14 percent, more common than 78 percent of the named colors we track, as photographed [5]. It peaks in the 1500s, at 2.0 times the expected rate (66 of 2,231 paintings from then), and inside a painting it plays an accent in 54 percent of cases, ranked by lightness rather than raw area [5]. André Derain is its most devoted painter here, using it in 5 of 22 works, 5.7 times the baseline for the museums those works come from [5]. It is most over-represented in Indian paintings, at 2.7 times the expected rate, and shares canvases with Reddish Orange well beyond chance [5]. The earliest match is dated 1150, 762 years before Ridgway's 1912 plate; the archive's early centuries are thin, so that date is a floor, not a first, and the match is a resemblance in an aged photograph, not proof any pigment existed then [5].
